n: Jesus warns against condemning others. He isn’t forbidding all judgment of right and wrong, but the harsh, self-righteous kind that writes people off.

f.g: The JST reads “Judge not unrighteously, that ye be not judged: but judge righteous judgment.”

n: The standard we use on others is the standard God will use on us. Merciful people receive mercy; harsh people invite harshness.

f.g: mete = measure out, as grain is measured in a container.

n: A deliberately funny picture: a man with a whole wooden beam stuck in his eye fussing over a speck of sawdust in someone else’s. We see others’ small faults while missing our own large ones.

f.g: mote = a tiny speck or splinter.
A large timber, like a roof rafter — intentional exaggeration.

n: Jesus presses the image further: how absurd to offer help with someone else’s speck while a beam blocks your own sight.

f.w: Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye

n: The fix is to deal honestly with our own sins first. Then, humbled and seeing clearly, we can actually help others instead of just criticizing them.

f.g: Greek hypokritēs — originally a stage actor wearing a mask; someone playing a part.

n: Sacred things should be shared with wisdom. Dogs and pigs (unclean animals to Jews) picture people who would mock or trample what is holy rather than receive it.

f.g: The JST adds that the mysteries of the kingdom are to be kept within oneself and not shared with the world.

n: A warm invitation to pray. The three verbs grow in effort — ask, seek, knock — and each comes with a promise that God will respond.

f.w: Ask, and it shall be given you

n: The promise is for “every one,” not just the important or righteous few. God hears every sincere seeker.
Jesus appeals to common sense: what parent would hand a hungry child a stone that looks like a loaf of bread?

f.g: Round flat loaves in Galilee could resemble stones, sharpening the contrast.

n: Or give a snake that looks a bit like a fish? No loving parent tricks a child like that.
The point lands here: if imperfect earthly parents give good gifts, our perfect Heavenly Father will be even more generous to those who ask.

f.g: Compared with God’s perfect goodness, all mortals fall short.

n: The “Golden Rule.” Treat others the way you want to be treated — Jesus says this sums up the whole message of the Old Testament.

f.g: A common name for the Hebrew scriptures as a whole.

n: There are two ways through life. The easy, popular road leads to ruin; it takes no effort to drift onto it.
The road to eternal life is narrow and demanding, and fewer people choose it — but it leads where we truly want to go.
Jesus warns of false teachers who look harmless and religious on the outside but are dangerous and greedy within.
The test of any teacher is the fruit of their life and teaching. Thornbushes never produce grapes; bad sources don’t produce truly good results.
Character shows itself over time. A healthy tree naturally bears good fruit; a rotten one bears bad fruit.
Jesus restates the principle firmly: what we really are inside eventually comes out in what we produce.

f.w: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit

n: Fruitless trees are cut down and burned — a sober image of final judgment, echoing John the Baptist’s preaching.

f.w: hewn down, and cast into the fire

n: Jesus closes the thought by repeating the key line: watch the fruit, and you will know the tree.

f.w: by their fruits ye shall know them

n: Calling Jesus “Lord” isn’t enough. Entrance into God’s kingdom comes to those who actually do the Father’s will.

f.w: doeth the will of my Father

n: At the judgment some will point to impressive religious works done in Christ’s name. Outward displays don’t substitute for a changed heart.
The heart of the matter is relationship. Those who never truly came to know Christ — though busy in his name — will hear, “I never knew you.”

f.g: The JST reads “Ye never knew me,” placing the failure on the hearers.

n: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with a parable. Hearing and then doing his words is like building a house on solid rock.
Storms come to everyone — rain, floods, wind. The house on the rock still stands because of what it’s founded on.

f.g: In Palestine, dry streambeds (wadis) could suddenly become torrents after heavy rain.

n: Hearing without doing is like building on sand. Everything may look fine until the storm comes.
The same storm hits, and this house collapses completely. The difference between the two builders was never the weather, but the foundation.

f.w: great was the fall of it

n: The crowd was amazed. Matthew marks the end of the sermon with a formula he uses after each of Jesus’s major discourses.

f.w: when Jesus had ended these sayings

n: Scribes taught by quoting earlier rabbis. Jesus spoke on his own authority — “I say unto you” — as the one who gave the law in the first place.

f.g: Professional experts who copied and interpreted the law of Moses.
